## Data Collection Instruments

The instruments below were developed over three years by working groups within
the Across the PONs collaborative and are openly available on the Open Science
Framework. They are free to use.

Our aim in developing them is simple. If enough scholars collect data on
purpose-oriented networks using common measures, the field gains a comparative
evidence base no single individual could build. Translations of the instruments and
codebooks into Spanish and Dutch are in progress. With other languages planned.

Instruments exist in parallel versions for the two policy domains, human services and environmental governance, since some
measures require domain-specific wording.

### PON Leader Interview Guide

A semi-structured interview guide for the network manager or convener, covering
the history of and motivation for the network, the environment it operates in,
its primary activities and theory of change, and how it is managed. This is
typically the entry point into a network, conducted before either survey. The
guide applies across policy domains, so a single version serves both human
services and environmental networks.

[View on OSF](https://osf.io/wkguq/overview)

### PON Leader Survey

A short survey of the network's leadership team, capturing mandate details,
resource munificence, and governance arrangements.

| Domain | Link |
|--------|------|
| Human services | [View on OSF](https://osf.io/3wg8p/overview) |
| Environmental | [View on OSF](https://osf.io/m4uj5/overview) |

### Organizational Member Survey

A survey of all organizational members of the network, capturing organizational
characteristics, member satisfaction and commitment, network functioning, and
member perceptions of network performance.

| Domain | Link |
|--------|------|
| Human services | [View on OSF](https://osf.io/n2x8m/overview) |
| Environmental | [View on OSF](https://osf.io/uhrz5/overview) |

## Using the Instruments

Scholars are welcome to deploy these instruments in their own research. The
collaborative operates under a data-use and sharing agreement that allows new
members to join and contribute cases to the shared database.

If you plan to use an instrument, or are interested in contributing data, please
contact members of the coordinating committee: 

{{< include _contact.qmd >}}

We can provide access to a Qualtrics version of the survey along with a guide on how to launch it with your particular PON.

## Working Papers


Alongside the instruments, the Across the PON's working groups have produced a
series of papers taking stock of the field and setting out directions for future
research.

### How the Forest Shapes the Trees: Context Mechanisms and Purpose-Oriented Networks

Context is usually treated as a static backdrop in PON research. This paper
argues instead that context is an active force that permeates network boundaries
and conditions their trajectories, and develops a framework identifying three
classes of contextual mechanism — norms, resources, and historical dynamics —
operating across five nested layers from the supranational to the community.

Albrecht, K., Raab, J., Sánchez, J., Nowell, B., Kapucu, N., Milward, H. B., &
Shumate, M. (April 2026).
[Read on SSRN](https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6959980)

### Linking Inputs to Network Dimensions in Purpose-Oriented Networks

Research on PONs has largely treated network structure as a predictor of
effectiveness. This paper reverses that direction, asking what gives rise to
different relational patterns in the first place, and links five inputs —
purpose, organizational capacity, resource munificence, degree of mandate, and
external stability — to network structure, composition, and dynamics.

Medina, A., Siciliano, M., Hu, Q., Morçöl, G., & Whetsell, T. (April 2026).
[Read on SSRN](https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7233618)

### From Modes to Myths: Untangling Governance, Management, and Institutional Elements in the Modes of Network Governance Typology

Provan and Kenis's governance mode typology remains the dominant framework for
analyzing how PONs are governed, yet what counts as governance — and how it
differs from network management — remains persistently ambiguous. Drawing on an
institutional perspective, this paper separates governance as constitutional and
collective-choice rules from management as operational process, and argues for
more rigorous justification of how governance modes are classified.

Sánchez, J., Lemaire, R., Mannak, R., Medina, A., van den Oord, S., Kenis, P.,
Kapucu, N., Milward, H. B., & Raab, J. (December 2025).
[Read on SSRN](https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7233380)
